content: The MOSAIC program provides a comprehensive range of services, including HIV counseling and testing through mobile services, couples testing, and home-based testing. It also offers diagnosis and treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), substance abuse treatment, mental health services, distribution of male and female condoms, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and linkage of HIV-positive men who have sex with men (MSM) to HIV care and treatment programs. Since its inception, the program has delivered HIV prevention services to 13,980 MSM, trained 2,010 healthcare workers in sensitivity training, provided clinical training to 269 clinicians, and offered ongoing mentorship to 24 health facilities. Anecdotal evidence suggests increased awareness of PrEP availability within the MSM community. The program operates under a monitoring and evaluation framework with specific indicators and targets, allowing for performance assessment and addressing gaps and challenges. Local engagement platforms, such as communities of practice, have enhanced coordination and effectiveness in MSM-focused programming. BCN Checkpoint, a community-based detection center in Barcelona's gay district, provides HIV, STI, and sexual health services for MSM. Managed by the NGO Projecte dels NOMS-Hispanosida, it offers free rapid HIV and syphilis testing by peers, hepatitis A and B vaccinations, referrals, and sexual health promotion. For individuals with HIV-positive results, the program provides immediate peer support and information from trained HIV-positive peer counselors, along with referrals to hospital HIV treatment units within one week. A register is maintained to ensure linkage to care for newly diagnosed individuals. To encourage annual repeat HIV testing, reminders are sent via email, text messages, and phone calls. Between 2007 and 2013, the program conducted over 22,000 HIV tests, identifying 756 new infections. Nearly 90% of clients are directly linked to care, 5% find their own care, and 4% obtain care in their home countries. Less than 2% of clients are lost to follow-up. The Adam’s Love website, launched in 2011, promotes regular HIV testing for MSM and links visitors to HIV testing and counseling (HTC) services through a section titled HIV Testing Site Near You, which provides information on MSM-friendly HTC sites in Bangkok and other provinces. The program also uses mass media, targeted media activities, peer-driven interventions, and celebrity HIV testing events to create demand for HTC services. The number of clients accessing HTC services increased nearly fivefold from 967 in 2008 to 4,371 in 2012. The website attracted over 500,000 visitors in two years and has a Facebook page with more than 15,000 fans. Twenty-five percent of Men’s Health Clinic clients reported seeking HTC services due to the site. The SASO program provides information and education on drug overdose management to people who inject drugs (PWID) and their families through small meetings, individual contacts, and counseling. The program was scaled up in 2008–09 to involve key stakeholders in community distribution of naloxone. Ethical concerns about non-medical staff dispensing naloxone were addressed by demonstrating its life-saving potential. Between 2004 and 2012, over 450 overdoses were managed at five centers, with a survival rate exceeding 90%. More than one-third of overdose clients accessed drug treatment and other healthcare services, such as HIV/HCV testing and antiretroviral therapy (ART). The HIV Cooperation Programme for Indonesia (HCPI) provides comprehensive HIV prevention and harm reduction services for PWID. It builds links with government health services to facilitate access to early HIV testing and treatment, basic healthcare, methadone maintenance treatment (MMT), needle and syringe programs (NSP), sexual and reproductive health services, and other necessary services. Activities are implemented through partnerships that leverage the strengths of community-based organizations (CBOs) and government structures. CBOs conduct outreach in hotspots, distribute condoms, provide prevention information, and refer clients to services. Public health centers and hospitals deliver therapeutic and preventive services, including MMT and NSP, along with safe injecting advice. Strong partnerships with law enforcement and government agencies enhance service delivery. Monthly data reporting and annual behavioral and satisfaction surveys are conducted to monitor program performance. The Muslim Education and Welfare Association (MEWA) provides HIV prevention and drug dependence treatment services in Kenya's Mombasa and Kilifi counties. The program improves access to clean needles and syringes, treatment, care, and socio-economic support services, while advocating for opioid substitution therapy and the human rights of key populations. It focuses on reuniting female drug users with their families, as family support enhances care engagement and retention. Free meals, reproductive health services, and basic social services are provided as incentives for service uptake. Clients on ART and TB treatment receive free accommodations to support adherence. MEWA also offers entrepreneurship training, job placement opportunities, and referrals to government agencies for micro-financing. The program supports children of drug users by arranging temporary custodial care and providing health, nutritional, material, and psychosocial support. Family reunification has been achieved for half of MEWA’s clients. The SIDC organization in Lebanon has provided harm reduction services since 1996 and outreach interventions since 1999. It launched the first drop-in center (DIC) in the Middle East for PWID in 2010, offering HTC, needle and syringe programs, opioid substitution therapy (OST), psychosocial and legal support, and advocacy to counter stigma and promote drug law reform. The program encourages parents to support OST for their children and collaborates with regional agencies to train stakeholders and service providers. Between 2010 and 2012, SIDC reached approximately 1,600 PWID, with 17% of OST patients in Lebanon managed by the program. However, OST is not free in Lebanon, limiting access for many PWID. Espolea, a youth-led organization in Mexico City, established a Drug Policy and Harm Reduction Programme in 2008. It provides practical, objective information about drugs and risk reduction to young people aged 15–29 through online and face-to-face channels. The organization disseminates information at events like music festivals and cultural gatherings, emphasizing risks, harms, and safer practices. Workshops are conducted in schools and communities with at-risk youth. Espolea uses social media for outreach and maintains blogs on various topics. The program addresses stigma around drug use through evidence-based publications and workshops with stakeholders and policymakers, promoting internationally accepted standards. It aims to reflect the needs of young people in policy and governmental action. The Nai Zindagi Trust in Pakistan has provided services to street-based PWID, their families, and children for 25 years. It collaborates with the public healthcare system to avoid parallel services, with 60% of services delivered by partner organizations. The program involves PWID community members in design, implementation, and evaluation, with 30–40% of outreach workers being former injectors. It prioritizes outreach over facility-based service delivery and offers harm reduction, HIV/STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and a residential ART adherence program. Skills training and employment opportunities are available for clients. A real-time management information system monitors service delivery and trends to adapt interventions. Since 2012, over 600 individuals have been trained to provide comprehensive services, supporting harm reduction for approximately 13,000 street-based PWID.
